To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
social services in the time of COVID 19 have developed smart welfare practices, but they are not yet smart enough.

the use of digital technologies has been a useful tool in supporting the social work practice in the field, but the use of digital technology is not enough to ensure the quality of the social services.

the use of new technology has allowed the continuation of social work services, even in the most critical moments of the emergency, but it has also highlighted the need to develop a new approach to social work that is more attentive to digital divide and to the need for social and relational proximity.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following aspects: 1) the use of digital technologies in the social and educational services in Italy during the COVID-19 emergency; 2) the role of social workers in the use of digital technology; 3) the impact on the quality and quantity of social services; 4) the impact on vulnerable people and families.

the following questions: How have social workers and families coped with the new situation? What are the strengths and weaknesses of the different local practices? What are the implications for future interventions?

the following issues: the use of new technology and social distancing in social services, the impact of COVID-19 on the relationship between the service and the user, the role of the social worker in the context of teleworking, the use of new communication tools, the impact of the pandemic on social work training.
Distant but Connected?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the smart welfare paradigm has been partially adopted, with a positive impact on some aspects and with some limitations and difficulties in others.
smart welfare, as an alternative to traditional welfare, is not a solution to all the problems, but it is a valid and effective tool in the hands of social workers.

, in the face of a global emergency like the COVID-19 pandemic, the smart welfare model has proved to be a valid tool for the continuity of social services, but the effectiveness of its implementation depends on the availability of adequate resources, on the capacity of social workers and on the ability of the local welfare system to adapt to the needs of vulnerable families and citizens.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social workers have been able to respond to the emergency, but that it has been difficult to maintain the same intensity of support to families.

the use of technology is an important resource to support social work and to ensure the continuity of social and educational services in the context of COVID 19 emergency, but it is not enough to guarantee the quality of services and to overcome the challenges of the digital divide.
the smart welfare is not a panacea but an opportunity to be used with caution and to be constantly evaluated and improved.
The main takeaway from our work is that

social and educational services, in the context of the COVID 19 emergency, can play a key role in supporting vulnerable families, but they need to be able to count on adequate and sustainable resources.

, although the pandemic has highlighted the importance of the digital divide, it has also highlighted how social services can be a privileged actor in the process of digital inclusion of the most vulnerable families and citizens.
social services should not be conceived as a substitute to face to face interventions but as a support for them, in a context of smart welfare where technology is used in a smart and careful way.
